Article Title: Uber, Instacart and Target can no longer charge you more based on your data in New York City; Mayor Zohran Mamdani says: New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against…
Article Text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

New York City Council passes law to ban surveillance pricing

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently shared a post on X (formerly Twitter) announcing a ban on “surveillance pricing” – a practice he says some companies use to charge different customers varying prices for identical goods or services. The City Council passed the legislation 44-5 on November 12, 2026, sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin with Mamdani's support; it targets data-driven price discrimination while allowing transparent loyalty programs and certain discounts. Notably, Uber , Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing.While many of the companies have denied using the practice, the new law seeks to prohibit it.“Some companies use your personal data, like browsing history, to serve different prices to different costumers. It’s called surveillance pricing, and we just banned it in New York City,” Mamdani wrote in the post.“This tweet will say the same thing in incognito mode, don’t worry,” he sarcastically said.The City Council on November 12 passed a bill to prohibit “surveillance pricing”. The new law bans companies from using browsing data to charge customers different prices for the same product.The surveillance pricing law passed the Democrat-dominated council in a 44-5 vote.“There are many factors that are driving up costs,” City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who sponsored the bill, said at City Hall ahead of the vote. “Some of them are quite obvious to consumers, but a more subtle reason is the insidious and predatory corporate practice of surveillance pricing.“For different consumers that are shopping at the exact same time, companies set different prices for the exact same product, taking advantage of their demographics, web browsing history, and shopping habits, as well as their social media activity, all to make New Yorkers pay more,” she added.If the companies fail to copley with the new surveillance law, they wil have to pay a fine of $1,000.
Article Summary: The City Council on November 12 passed a bill to prohibit “surveillance pricing” The new law bans companies from using browsing data to charge customers different prices for the same product. Article Title: Microsoft outage hits AI tools of Anthropic and OpenAI, companies’ Status Page give details
Article Text:
OpenAI: Microsoft connectors in ChatGPT

Anthropic: Microsoft 365 connector and Claude for Outlook

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft reports 'positive results' in fix for Outlook, Teams and other 365 services

A massive Microsoft outage which disrupted Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other workplace applications has also affected Microsoft integrations used by ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and Claude-creator Anthropic. Both the AI companies have reported issued with their Microsoft 365 connectors on their respective service-status pages as Microsoft continues to work in order to restore its services. OpenAI said that the new connections to Microsoft connectors could fail and that exiting tools might also not work as expected. On the other hand, Anthropic also reported problems with its Microsoft 365 connectors, attributing the disruption to an upstream provider.OpenAI’s status page opened an incident titled “Elevated errors affecting the Microsoft 365 connector.” It said OpenAI was investigating an issue in which new connections to Microsoft connectors might be broken and tools might not work as expected. The first update was posted on Thursday, November 12, at 1:29 p.m., and the affected component was ChatGPT’s Connectors/Apps. The page showed degraded performance and only the initial “investigating” update when I opened it, with no fix or cause stated.Anthropic’s status page logged an incident with the same title, beginning at 17:52 UTC (12:52 p.m. ET). It first reported elevated errors and slow responses affecting requests to mail, SharePoint, Teams chat and calendar through the connector, and said new connections might not complete.By 18:34 UTC the company said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider. Mail, calendar and search tools were failing for most requests. A later update said Claude for Outlook was also affected: mail and calendar actions might fail, and some users might not be able to open the add-in.At 21:18 UTC, Anthropic said it was working with the upstream provider, which was restarting affected servers. At 22:23 UTC (5:23 p.m. ET), the latest update on the page said the issue was caused by a Microsoft 365 service incident and the tools were still failing for most requests. It pointed users to Microsoft’s status page for progress and said it would update when service was restored. The incident was still listed as unresolved.The page also showed claude.ai and Claude Cowork as degraded. The Claude API, Claude Code and Claude Console were listed as operational, so the problem appears limited to the Microsoft-dependent features.Microsoft says its fix for the global Microsoft 365 outage is finally starting to work. More than 12 hours after users around the world lost access to Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services, the company said on Friday that it is seeing "positive results" for server stability. A full recovery, however, is still some way off.In its latest update on the Microsoft 365 service health page, the company said it has applied an "upstream authentication/routing configuration component patch" to a portion of its infrastructure. Put simply, the fix targets how users connect to Microsoft's servers. Microsoft said it will keep monitoring the patch and is working to roll it out to servers supporting active regions as they come back online. There is still no timeline for when services will be fully restored.
Article Summary: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and Claude-creator Anthropic report problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors. OpenAI said that the new connections to Microsoft connectors could fail and that exiting tools might also not work as expected. Anthropic also reported problems with its Microsoft 365 connector, attributing the disruption to an upstream provider.

Article Title: Meta’s head of Infrastructure, Engineering Santosh Janardhan is leaving the company after 15 years; says in an internal memo: Time to pass ...
Article Text:
A long-time Amazon's cloud unit executive, Dave Brown joined Meta in July 2026

Meta Platforms' longtime infrastructure head will leave the company in early 2027. Santosh Janardhan, Meta’s head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, told the company's employees that he would step down from leading the infrastructure organization, according to a memo obtained by Bloomberg News. He did not detail the reasons for his departure in the message.Janardhan, who has worked at Meta since 2009, said “it’s time to pass the baton” to former AWS senior vice president David Brown , who joined Meta in July from AWS. Janardhan said in the memo that he will help support Brown through the first quarter of 2027 as part of “the transition.” He wrote, “As we make the next set of choices about our priorities, this is the right time for Dave to take the lead in shaping that work." Janardhan added in the memo, “Dave has spent his career building and operating dependable infrastructure for a wide range of demanding workloads. He has the instincts, depth and judgment this moment requires.”The announcement means that Brown will now formally lead Meta’s infrastructure efforts and serve as chief technical officer of the Meta Compute initiative, which is spearheaded by the company’s president and vice chairman Dina Powell McCormick and technical leader Daniel Gross.Dave Brown joined Meta in July 2026. Previously, he was senior vice president in Amazon Web Services. Brown joined AWS in its initial days and was a member of the early team that assembled its core EC2 service in South Africa in the 2000s. EC2, one of AWS’ oldest services, provides virtual slices of physical servers for rent, billed by the second, that companies use to run applications and websites. He was also part of Amazon CEO Andy Jassy’s S-team. Jassy's S-team is reported to be a highly influential group of 28 executives with whom CEO Jassy meets regularly to make key business decisions.According to analysts, the change of guard underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s efforts to expand the company’s data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals.This major leadership change comes as Meta continues to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to support it.During its third quarter earnings report, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, said, "We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone - including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model.” It added that it expects full-year capex to fall in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. Meta also logged negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, which S&P Global Ratings noted as part of its decision in late October to revise Meta’s credit rating from AA- stable to AA- negative.
Article Summary: Santosh Janardhan, Meta’s head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, told the company's employees that he would step down from leading the infrastructure organization. He did not detail the reasons for his departure in the message. Dave Brown joined Meta in July from Amazon Web Services.

Article Title: Microsoft outage: Airlines issue advisory; Australia's spy agency, police impacted; key points
Article Text:
More than 12 hours after the US technology giant first reported the issue, its engineers were still struggling to restore services fully

Here are the top developments from the global

Microsoft outage

:

Hong Kong banking services disrupted: Employees at major financial institutions, including Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs, reported disruptions to their work after being unable to access emails and Microsoft Teams. Speaking to CNN, one banker said some emails were arriving sporadically, but millions of messages were potentially stuck in a backlog. The disruption also affected businesses relying on communications with overseas customers.

Australian government services, schools affected: Schools, courts and government services in Australia experienced disruptions as employees struggled to access Outlook and other Microsoft applications. Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft had compared the incident to the CrowdStrike outage of July 2024. Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator. Microsoft did not believe it was dealing with a cyberattack and suspected an update-related problem, he said.

Japan turns to physical documents: The outage affected government IT infrastructure in Japan, with ministries and agencies struggling to send emails through much of Friday's working day. Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said government employees were responding by making physical copies of documents. He added that authorities were closely monitoring developments.

Philippine courts report delays: The Supreme Court of the Philippines said the Microsoft 365 disruption had affected some of its operations. In a post on X, it warned that responses to emails and other transactions could be delayed while the disruption continued.

Singapore government emails affected: Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it was working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.

Indian airlines report email disruptions: IndiGo said the outage had affected its email support services, limiting its ability to receive customer queries. However, its other customer support channels remained operational and flight operations were unaffected. Akasa Air issued an advisory informing passengers about delays in its email support services.

US businesses face disruption: Several US city governments reported widespread email problems and advised residents to contact local offices by phone where necessary. Industrial technology company Workhorse Group postponed its quarterly earnings conference call because of the disruption.

AI platforms report connectivity issues: OpenAI and Anthropic also reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, highlighting the wider impact of the outage on platforms that rely on integrations with other companies' software.

What we know about the Microsoft outage

Microsoft's global outage continued to disrupt businesses and government operations across several countries on Friday, with banking services affected in Hong Kong, government systems facing problems in Australia and Japan, and courts reporting delays in the Philippines. The disruption, which began on Thursday, has left millions of users struggling to access essential services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams and other Microsoft 365 applications.More than 12 hours after the US technology giant first reported the issue, its engineers were still struggling to restore services fully. Microsoft reported some progress but acknowledged that attempts to improve serviceability were not working as expected. The company said it had found no evidence of malicious activity behind the disruption.Microsoft said the disruption was affecting a broad range of Microsoft 365 services that interact with its Exchange Online and email infrastructure. Outlook, Teams and its AI assistant Copilot were among the services users reported having trouble accessing.The company said it was taking a measured approach to identifying and repairing the affected infrastructure while exploring different ways to determine the cause of the problem and restore services.The outage spread rapidly, with tracking website Downdetector recording disruptions across 74 countries and territories within roughly an hour. More than 130,000 users reported problems accessing Outlook at the peak of the disruption on Thursday.Microsoft initially reported that it had made progress in restoring service health and functionality. However, a subsequent update indicated that the changes were not delivering the expected results."We've monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they're not taking as expected," Microsoft said in an update on X.The company said it was identifying alternative workstreams to address the disruption and would continue treating the incident with urgency until services were fully restored.
Article Summary: Microsoft outage continues to disrupt businesses and government operations across several countries. Outage has left millions of users struggling to access essential services, including Outlook, Microsoft Teams and other Microsoft 365 applications. More than 12 hours after the US technology giant first reported the issue, its engineers were still struggling to restore services fully.

Article Title: Nvidia employees want Jensen Huang back as CEO; internal suggestion box post draws over 1,600 comments: We are all humans and can make mistakes, Jensen did so many good things and he...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang.

Nvidia employee's companywide email backs Jensen Huang

Why Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO

Nvidia staff say the company needs its founder

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jensen Huang may have stepped down as Nvidia CEO, but a large part of the company's workforce isn't ready to move on. An internal suggestion box post urging Nvidia's board to weigh employee sentiment before deciding Huang's future has drawn more than 1,600 comments, with most of them backing his return to the top job, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired.The post was written by a longtime Nvidia engineer before Huang resigned. It has since become a rallying point for staff who want the 63-year-old cofounder reinstated, despite the multiple reported extramarital affairs that led to his abrupt exit. "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," wrote one anonymous commenter. Another added, "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance. "The support hasn't stayed inside the suggestion box. One employee sent an email to the entire company demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "I stand by Jensen," the staffer wrote. "Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us."The same email went a step further: "If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang."The employee behind the email couldn't be reached for comment, while the engineer who wrote the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, Harvey Jones, did not immediately respond to Wired's requests for comment.Huang, who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote to employees on Sunday admitting he had been "unfaithful to [his] wife" and that there was "no excuse." The email followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.The board announced his resignation on Thursday morning, after reports of an alleged second affair, this time with a direct report. That employee has not commented on the matter. Reuters has since reported an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn't said anything about these reports since his Sunday email.The fallout has been heavy. Nvidia has lost about $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced. US lawmakers and the FBI have opened investigations, and the episode has raised the prospect of fresh export controls on chips. The board, made up largely of early Nvidia investors and Huang's longtime confidants, has named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. Former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones is the new chair.Work inside Nvidia has carried on as usual this week, but the resignation left many employees stunned. Within hours, about two dozen staffers posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one calling their faith in his leadership unwavering. Over the same period, Wired couldn't find a single post from an Nvidia employee supporting his exit.One employee, who has been at the company for a couple of years and wasn't authorised to speak publicly, told Wired the push for Huang's reinstatement is widespread. They worry Nvidia will suffer in the long run without its founder in charge and say the board must bring him back. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," the employee said.Much of the frustration comes down to timing. Many employees expected the board's investigation to wrap up before any big changes were made. The suggestion box post had asked the board to share its findings with staff and formally gather their views "about Jensen's continuing as our CEO."That never happened. Huang stepped down just as the inquiry had begun, and staff are still looking for answers on why he left before it was done.
Article Summary: Internal post urges Nvidia board to weigh employee sentiment before deciding Huang's future. One employee sent an email to the entire company demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang," the employee wrote.

Microsoft 365 is facing a widespread outage that has disrupted access to Outlook, Teams, Microsoft Copilot and other services, affecting users trying to access emails, workplace tools and cloud-based applications. The disruption started on November 12 and has continued into November 13, with the company saying it is still working to restore services after its initial fixes failed to deliver a recovery. According to Microsoft’s service health advisories, users may experience email delivery delays, problems loading Copilot Chat and failures in Teams features linked to Exchange Online. Microsoft says it is scaling up virtual machines and investigating traffic imbalances as it works to address the issue.As per Microsoft's service health advisories, the Microsoft 365 outage has impacted the following services:- Exchange Online: Users may be unable to access their mailbox using Outlook on the web, Outlook desktop (MAPI), Exchange ActiveSync (EAS), or REST-based connections, and email delivery may be delayed.Admins may be unable to load some admin center pages.Users may be unable to view their recently used files.Multiple services including Cloud Update, Cloud Policy, and Inventory are affected.Features including Assignments, Reading Progress, and Speaker Progress may be impacted.Users may be unable to load Copilot Chat or receive responses in the web and desktop apps, and Copilot experiences may be unable to access work data such as email, calendar, and files.Failures may occur for scenarios including access to Safe Links, Safe Attachments, protection and submission policies, and attempts to view Quarantine, Threat Explorer, and Email remediation events. Additionally, delays may occur for Tenant Allow / Block list changes, unified Role-Based Access Control, reporting, message traces, content extraction, and outbound protection. Users clicking on wrapped/rewritten URLs typically processed by Safe Links will result in a failure to navigate, as Safe Links fails to process it. Users who are able to successfully access the Quarantine portal may encounter failures when attempting to release items from quarantine.Users may be unable to load Microsoft Defender portal pages or solution tabs.Users may encounter failures when exporting reports with sensitivity labels to PDF or PowerPoint, when updating artifacts with sensitivity labels, or opening pbix with sensitivity label in Power BI Desktop. As a workaround, users can remove the sensitivity label from the affected item to complete the operation, if their organization's data protection policies allow it.API requests that access Exchange Online data, such as mail, calendar, and contacts, may time out and prevent users from managing Teams, Channels, Membership, Apps management and send activity notifications using Graph API.Scenarios including device enrollment, device check-in, and device compliance policies may have been intermittently impacted.Users are experiencing Plan and Task operation reliability issues.Multiple Purview services including Authorization, auto-labeling, Data Loss Prevention (DLP) across Microsoft 365 services, Communication Compliance, Information Protection label and auto-labeling policies, Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and Data Classification are impacted, and users may be unable to open or load Microsoft Purview portal pages or protected content. Audit searches, protected content creation, eDiscovery tasks such as search and export, Data Classification and On Demand Scan features may also be impacted.Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats. Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.The app may not load, and users may see operation failures.All users may intermittently be unable to export reports with MIP sensitivity labels to PDF in Power BI.Features that depend on Exchange Online may be impacted. Accessing files stored directly in SharePoint Online remains functional.Users may encounter errors submitting print jobs or using admin features.Customers who have configured their tenant and Cloud PCs to use Microsoft Purview Customer Key for Windows 365 Cloud PCs may have users who are unable to connect to their Cloud PCs.As stated on the status page, Microsoft says it has “applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers. Article Title: 'Servers remain stable so far': Microsoft begins restoring services after global outage hits 365 suite

Microsoft has begun restoring services after a widespread global outage disrupted access to its Microsoft 365 suite, including Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and OneDrive.The company said a portion of the affected servers had been returned to service and remained stable so far, while it was shifting traffic to alternative routes to ease the disruption."We're returning a portion of affected servers to the service, and they remain stable so far," Microsoft said in an update. It added that it had observed limited recovery after moving traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible.The company said it had also streamlined the process of bringing the remaining affected servers back online. However, it cautioned that servers restored to service could become unresponsive again once they started receiving traffic."In parallel, we're temporarily limiting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in some locations," Microsoft said.The outage affected Microsoft's email, workplace communication and cloud-based services, with nearly 130,000 users worldwide reporting problems at the peak, according to outage tracker Downdetector.Users reported difficulties accessing Outlook, sending and receiving emails and loading inboxes. Thousands also reported disruptions to Teams, Microsoft's AI assistant Copilot and other Microsoft 365 applications.Microsoft initially said it was investigating reports of users experiencing problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods.The company later identified elevated load across part of its infrastructure as a likely reason for the connectivity errors. It said several servers had become unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks, shifting additional traffic onto the remaining infrastructure.Microsoft said the elevated load was not being caused by an overall increase in traffic, but by the reduced availability of servers.In its recovery updates, Microsoft said it had validated an alternative health-check method on a subset of affected servers, allowing them to return to service. It then began applying the fix more widely.The company also worked on an automated process to detect and restart unresponsive servers. A review of recent changes identified configuration updates as a possible cause of the disruption, although the investigation was continuing.Microsoft said it had paused deployments and configuration changes while examining whether recent updates were linked to the outage.The company also said a core process on the affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, causing them to stop responding. Earlier recovery measures had not provided the expected relief, prompting it to pursue additional ways to restore services.Microsoft had earlier reported that it had successfully restored issues affecting Teams in North America, although some users continued to experience connectivity problems, according to news agency AP.The company has not provided a definitive cause for the wider outage in the updates.Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University, told The Guardian that the disruption appeared to be affecting the network layer of Microsoft's systems.He said the unavailability of some servers could force users to rely on a smaller pool of remaining infrastructure, increasing the load on those servers and potentially causing further failures.Gregory described this as a "cascading problem" and said identifying the underlying issue, which he suggested could involve a network configuration problem, would take time.He also said companies should invest in testing environments for configuration changes before deploying them on live networks. Businesses relying on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should maintain alternative options, he added.The outage also affected integrations connecting AI services to Microsoft's platforms. OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the Microsoft 365 connectors used by ChatGPT and Claude, respectively, according to The Guardian.Microsoft said customers could experience a gradual recovery as users reconnect to its services.
Article Summary: Outage affected Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and OneDrive. Nearly 130,000 users worldwide reported problems at the peak, according to outage tracker Downdetector. Microsoft said a portion of the affected servers had been returned to service and remained stable so far.

Article Title: Jensen Huang joins Steve Jobs, Jack Dorsey in list of tech founders who lost top jobs

Jensen Huang - founder of graphics-chip maker Nvidia - has stepped down as the company's president, CEO and board member following reports of two alleged affairs. One of the reported relationships involved a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of spying for Beijing.In a statement, Nvidia said its board had selected current vice-president Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO until a permanent successor is appointed."Kress will continue to serve as executive vice-president and chief financial officer while serving as interim chief executive officer until a permanent successor has been named. The board is initiating a search for a permanent chief executive officer and will consider internal and external candidates," the statement said."Jensen's contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry," it added.Huang's exit adds another name to the list of tech founders who have been forced out of companies they built, following controversies, boardroom battles or internal differences.Here is a look at founders who lost control of the companies they once founded.Steve Jobs co-founded Apple with Steve Wozniak in 1976, starting the company from his family's garage in California. In less than five years, Apple went public in 1981 as it rapidly grew into a major technology company.In 1983, Jobs recruited PepsiCo executive John Sculley as CEO."Do you want to sell sugar water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world?" Jobs famously asked him.In 1984, Apple's Macintosh debuted to rave reviews but disappointing sales, triggering internal tensions within the company. Differences emerged between Jobs and Sculley over the computer's performance, management style and Jobs' demanding approach towards employees. Jobs had also built a separate team for the Macintosh, creating friction within the company.The differences eventually triggered a power struggle. In the spring of 1985, Apple's board backed Sculley and stripped Jobs of his leadership role in the Macintosh division. Jobs left Apple later that year, going on to establish NeXT and invest in Pixar. Apple eventually acquired NeXT in 1996, paving the way for his return.Jack Dorsey co-founded Twitter in 2006 alongside Biz Stone, Evan Williams and Noah Glass. He became the company's first CEO in 2007, but his leadership came under criticism after the social media platform struggled with technical problems and questions over his management style.In 2008, Twitter's board replaced Dorsey with fellow co-founder Evan Williams as CEO. Dorsey was moved to the position of chairman, effectively ending his operational control of the company.However, Dorsey returned to Twitter as interim CEO in 2015 after Dick Costolo stepped down. He was appointed permanent CEO in September that year, while continuing to lead payments company Square, which he had co-founded in 2009.His second stint also ended in November 2021 when he announced his resignation. The board appointed then CTO Parag Agrawal as his successor.Explaining his departure, Dorsey said he believed Twitter was ready to move on from its founders. Unlike his 2008 exit, his 2021 departure was announced as a decision he had made himself.Sachin and Binny Bansal founded Flipkart in 2007 as an online bookstore, turning it into one of India's biggest e-commerce companies.In January 2016, Sachin stepped down as CEO and was replaced by Binny amid investor concerns over the company's performance and strategy. Sachin remained executive chairman.Binny took over as group CEO but resigned in November 2018 following an independent investigation into allegations of personal misconduct. He denied the allegations.Walmart, which had acquired a 77% stake in Flipkart earlier that year, said the investigation found no evidence to substantiate the complainant's claims but identified other lapses of judgement.Jerry Yang co-founded Yahoo with David Filo in 1994 and became its CEO in June 2007.In 2008, Yang rejected Microsoft's $44.6-billion acquisition offer, arguing that it undervalued the company. The decision triggered criticism from shareholders, particularly after negotiations collapsed and Yahoo's share price continued to fall.Under pressure from investors and the board, Yang announced in November 2008 that he would step down as CEO once a successor was appointed. He remained on the board and returned to the role of "Chief Yahoo".In January 2012, he resigned from Yahoo's board and all other positions, ending his association with the company.Sam Altman, who co-founded OpenAI in 2015, was abruptly fired as CEO by the company's board on November 17, 2023. The board said he had not been consistently candid in his communications, affecting its ability to fulfil its responsibilities.His removal triggered an internal revolt, with hundreds of employees threatening to quit unless the board reinstated him. Microsoft, OpenAI's biggest investor, also offered Altman a position to lead a new advanced AI research team.After days of negotiations, OpenAI agreed to bring Altman back as CEO on November 21, with a reconstituted board. He officially returned on November 29, 2023.Travis Kalanick co-founded Uber in 2009 and built it into one of the world's biggest ride-hailing companies. However, his aggressive leadership style and a series of controversies eventually cost him his job.In 2017, Uber faced allegations of sexual harassment, workplace discrimination and a toxic corporate culture. An internal investigation led by former US attorney general Eric Holder recommended sweeping changes.The crisis deepened after a video surfaced showing Kalanick arguing with an Uber driver over fare cuts. He later apologised for his behaviour.In June 2017, five major investors, including Benchmark Capital, demanded his resignation. Kalanick eventually stepped down as CEO, saying he had accepted the investors' request. He remained on Uber's board.

Article Title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO: Who takes over, what lies ahead, and why the trouble isn’t over for Huang and Nvidia
Article Text:
Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has resigned as CEO

Colette Kress is interim CEO, so who runs Nvidia next and why Jensen Huang is hard to replace

Alice Huang spy investigation, FBI and Congress: Jensen Huang's troubles are not over

What Jensen Huang's exit means for US chip export controls, China and the AI boom

Nvidia stock and Q3 earnings: What investors will watch on November 17

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nvidia went 33 years without ever having to say who would follow Jensen Huang. That is now the company's most urgent question, and it has to be answered with the share price falling and the world watching. Colette Kress is minding the shop as interim CEO while directors look for a permanent chief. Investigators in Washington are still digging, and the push to sell American AI chips to China has lost the executive who argued for it hardest.The board removed the preeminent face of the AI infrastructure boom after reports of two affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China. Huang fought to keep his job, The New York Times reported, but plans for Kress to step in were already in motion by Wednesday.Nvidia shares tumbled a little more than 14% after the opening bell to $148.80, their lowest price since June 2025. The stock has since clawed back some ground and was trading at about $166.30, down roughly 7% for the day, at the time of writingKress was always meant to be a bridge. She will run the company and its finances at the same time, and the search for a permanent chief is open to outsiders as well as insiders. Directors had been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements even before the announcement, a sign the board had planned for this outcome.A shortlist has already taken shape. Analysts and investors keep coming back to two internal names: Kress and Ian Buck, the engineer who runs product for hyperscale AI. Outside names include Arm chief Rene Haas, who previously worked at Nvidia, and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji. Jeff Fisher, a 32-year Nvidia veteran, has also come up. Minotaur Capital's Armina Rosenberg has suggested a split arrangement, with a finance-minded leader such as Kress sharing the top job with a technologist such as Buck.The difficulty is less about names than about how Nvidia was built. Huang has said he is opposed to succession planning. He managed more than 60 direct reports, a flat setup that will be hard to unwind. He once said traditional org charts made no sense to him, and he claimed to read several thousand emails a day. His Santa Clara office is built around an enormous oval desk facing his lieutenants, with stadium seating behind them.Money is tied to his name too. Nvidia sits on about $99 billion in equity investments, spread across frontier AI labs, neoclouds and infrastructure firms. In August, it lined up more than $500 billion in data centre financing with six large financial institutions. Morningstar's Brian Colello wrote this week that it is unclear what those arrangements look like under another CEO, and that borrowing could get costlier without Huang orchestrating them. Futurum Equities' Shay Boloor framed the long-term risk around vision: Huang has been the person who consistently identified where computing is going.Leaving Nvidia does not take Huang out of the line of fire. The board's own inquiry, run with the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen and Katz, has an uncertain future now that its subject has gone. The federal investigations are wider. The Justice Department is running several probes that touch on Alice Huang, The Wall Street Journal reported, and Trump said on Monday that the FBI was examining the relationship.New detail has emerged on how long Washington knew. According to the Times, a classified memo overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated among officials before Trump's China trip in May, warning that the Megaspeed executive was allegedly working for China's Ministry of State Security. Trump had also reportedly been briefed about her roughly a year ago and chose not to act.Then there is the money trail. Megaspeed's sister company in Malaysia spent $4.8 billion or more on Nvidia chips and technology between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records cited by the Times. That is an unusually large bill for a small firm, at a time when Nvidia hardware is rationed. Both companies deny wrongdoing, and Beijing has dismissed the claims as "nothing but smears."Capitol Hill is next in line. In a November 4 letter, the Republican chairs of three House committees asked Huang to a closed-door briefing on November 18. They want to know about his dealings with Alice Huang and whether Beijing shaped Nvidia's decisions or US chip export policy. Lawmakers have also raised the threat of a subpoena.The board's ability to act was never in doubt. Nvidia has one class of stock with one vote per share, and independent directors hold 10 of its 11 seats. Unlike the founders of Meta or Alphabet, Huang had no super-voting shares to protect his job.The biggest effects may show up in policy. Huang was corporate America's leading advocate of selling to China, and in 2025 he called US export curbs "a failure." His pitch was that American chips in Chinese data centres would make US technology the global standard. In July 2025, he made that case to Trump in the Oval Office, and days later H20 sales to China were cleared. By December, Trump allowed sales to approved Chinese buyers, with the US government taking a 25% cut.The lobbying and the scandal are separate things. CSET analyst Hanna Dohmen has noted that Nvidia had every commercial reason to push for looser rules, intelligence operation or not, since each restriction caps its sales. The affair has still damaged the messenger. A trio of bills to restrict chip sales abroad has gained momentum. One of them, already passed by the House and awaiting the Senate, would extend controls to cloud computing, stopping Chinese firms from renting advanced Nvidia servers in countries such as Malaysia. Chinese AI stocks fell on Thursday on fears that their access to top-end chips could narrow.The White House has not turned on him. Trump called Huang "an honorable guy" and said he had "done an amazing job for our country." Huang's financial grip on Nvidia also remains large even without a board seat. More than half of his 922 million shares sit in a trust he co-manages with his wife, Lori. Elon Musk has said he would be open to hiring him.Kress faces her first public test within a week. Nvidia reports third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on November 17, with the earnings call at 2 pm PT, or 3:30 am IST on November 18. She has sat beside Huang on these calls for years. On this one, analysts will spend as much time on leadership as on data centre revenue.The sell side moved before the board did. As reports of Huang's likely removal surfaced on Wednesday night, Bernstein downgraded the stock and halved its target from $400 to $200. Oppenheimer dropped its target entirely and warned of a possible "brain drain," and Evercore cut its target to $186 from $330. Earlier in the week, tech analyst Dan Ives had already put a number on the Huang premium: $300 a share with him, $225 without.Estimates are that the slide could erase roughly $1 trillion from Nvidia's market value this month alone.There is a bull case, and it rests on the product pipeline. Blackwell demand, the Rubin roadmap, networking and the CUDA software ecosystem were all locked in before the scandal, which is why some analysts want the leadership crisis kept apart from the business.The board has promised continuity. Whether Nvidia's customers, lenders and engineers believe it will become clearer on November 17, when a company that has spoken in Huang's voice since 1993 reports for the first time without him.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993, has resigned as CEO. Colette Kress is interim CEO while directors look for a permanent chief. Investigators in Washington are still digging, and the push to sell American AI chips to China has lost the executive who argued for it hardest.

Article Title: Fireflies.ai expands beyond AI meeting notes with launch of AI teammate 'Fred', unveils first hardware device

Moving beyond meeting notes

New tools span scheduling, email and enterprise search

Fireflies unveils first hardware product

Adoption growing rapidly

Pricing and availability

Fireflies.ai has announced its biggest product expansion to date, transforming its platform from an AI meeting assistant into a broader workplace productivity suite centred around a new AI teammate called "Fred". The company said the upgraded platform will help users manage tasks across meetings, email, Slack, scheduling, screen recording and more than 240 connected applications. The announcement was made by Krish Ramineni, co-founder and CEO of Fireflies.ai, during a keynote presentation, where the company also unveiled a refreshed brand identity and offered a first look at Fireflies Fly, its first hardware product.Fireflies.ai, which says it is now used by more than 1 million organisations and teams at 75% of Fortune 500 companies, originally built its reputation around AI-powered meeting transcription and note-taking. The company is now expanding into a broader set of productivity tools designed to help employees manage work before, during and after meetings.According to Fireflies, demand for AI assistance beyond meeting notes has grown rapidly.The company said usage of Fred for non-meeting tasks increased 140% over the past six months, while the AI assistant completed nearly 100 million tasks during the same period."For years, Fred has joined your meetings, taken notes and helped with follow-ups. Now he's ready for a promotion," said Krish Ramineni. "Most teams pay for separate tools for meeting notes, scheduling, email assistants, Slack bots, voice typing and enterprise search. We're bringing these capabilities together in Fireflies under one subscription."The expanded Fireflies platform includes a range of new features designed to centralise workplace workflows. Among the additions are Fireflies Scheduler, a free scheduling tool with booking links and calendar management capabilities; Fireflies Talk, which offers voice typing and voice-based commands; and Fireflies Clips, a screen-recording tool that automatically generates transcripts, summaries and documentation.The company has also expanded Fred's capabilities across email and Slack, allowing the AI assistant to organise inboxes, draft responses, summarise channels and assist with routine tasks. A new Knowledge Search feature enables employees to search across meetings, documents, emails, Slack messages and connected applications from a single interface.Fireflies also introduced FredBots, which can be assigned recurring responsibilities such as competitor monitoring, customer feedback analysis and follow-up tasks, and Voice Agents capable of handling candidate screenings, sales calls, customer support interactions and user interviews.Alongside its software announcements, Fireflies revealed Fireflies Fly, a compact hardware device that attaches to the back of a smartphone and can take notes during phone calls, WhatsApp calls and in-person conversations. The company said the device is intended to help users capture conversations outside traditional video meetings, while emphasising that users should always comply with local recording laws and inform participants when recording.Fireflies highlighted strong growth across several newer products. The company said Email Assistant usage increased 25-fold in a single quarter, while adoption tripled over the same period. Voice Agents are now being used by thousands of businesses in more than 50 countries and support dozens of languages, according to the company. Fireflies also reported that adoption of its Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem increased fourfold in six months, with tens of millions of actions completed through MCP integrations and AI agents during the past quarter.A customer testimonial from vCommission cited significant time savings from Fireflies Voice Agents, with the company's HR team reportedly reducing the number of employee check-ins requiring direct human involvement.As Fireflies expands access to workplace data across multiple applications, the company stressed its privacy commitments. Co-founder and CTO Sam Udotong said Fireflies does not use customer content to train generative AI models and that users retain ownership of their data. Enterprise customers can also use private storage options and set their own retention policies."An AI teammate becomes more useful when it understands the context behind your work. But that should never come at the expense of customers losing control," said Sam Udotong.The new Fireflies experience is available starting today, with several features rolling out over the coming weeks. Waitlists are now open for FredBots, Fireflies Scheduler, Fireflies Clips and Fireflies Fly, while the hardware device is expected to become available early next year.Fireflies will continue to offer a free plan that includes meeting notes and core capabilities such as scheduling, voice typing and screen recording. Paid plans start at $10 per user per month when billed annually, with advanced features including email and Slack assistants, Voice Agents, FredBots and additional connected tools.
Article Summary: Fireflies.ai has announced its biggest product expansion to date, transforming its platform from an AI meeting assistant into a broader workplace productivity suite. The company said the upgraded platform will help users manage tasks across meetings, email, Slack, scheduling, screen recording and more than 240 applications. Fireflies also introduced FredBots, which can be assigned recurring responsibilities such as competitor monitoring, customer feedback analysis and follow-up tasks.

Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia’s President and CEO and has also left the company’s board, with immediate effect. Nvidia’s board announced his exit on Thursday, November 12, and named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. Kress will keep her CFO role until the board finds a permanent replacement.The resignation follows weeks of mounting pressure on the 63-year-old, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led it through the AI boom. On Sunday, November 8, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed. US officials reportedly suspect her of spying for China. On Wednesday, fresh reports said he had also had a relationship with a married healthcare executive at Nvidia who reported to him. Nvidia’s announcement does not give a reason for his exit.Kress has been Nvidia’s CFO since September 2013. Before that, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft. The board said it will consider both internal and external candidates for the permanent job.Nvidia has also appointed Harvey C. Jones as the first-ever Chair of its board. Jones is a former CEO and Executive Chairman of chip design software maker Synopsys. He said the board hasand expects the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmapKress said she is committed toThe board called Huang’s contributionsand thanked him for hisThe trouble started with reports that US intelligence agencies believed Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was passing information to Beijing. She is not related to Jensen Huang. Megaspeed is an Nvidia customer and has separately faced scrutiny over whether it helped restricted AI chips reach China. Beijing has denied using her to spy on Huang.At first, Huang played it down. On October 29, he described his interactions with her asthe kind he has with many Chinese customers and executives. Ten days later, he wrote to employees:Nvidia’s board then opened an independent investigation, overseen by a committee of independent directors with outside counsel. It said Huang would stay on as CEO and that it had no reason to believe company secrets had been compromised. Huang was also reportedly facing an FBI investigation over the relationship.The fallout spread quickly. Nvidia shares fell nearly 7% in under a week, sliding to eight-month lows over national security concerns, and a proposed class action lawsuit accused the company of misleading shareholders about Huang’s ties to Alice Huang.Wednesday’s report then added a separate problem. A relationship with someone who reported to him appears to go against Nvidia’s code of conduct. The board met that night to decide his future, and the White House was reportedly aware of the meeting. Less than a day later, Huang was out.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia's President and CEO. He has also left the company's board, with immediate effect. Nvidia’s board announced his exit on Thursday, November 12, and named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. Kress will keep her CFO role until the board finds a permanent replacement.

Article Title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp, a $2 million Republican donor whose software powers ICE deportations, says: I’ve been a Democrat my whole life, I know more about being a...
Article Text:
Alex Karp calls Palantir’s products “essentially progressive”

Alex Karp says his political donations were always balanced

Why Palantir’s CEO is warming up to Democrats after the midterms

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Palantir CEO Alex Karp wants Washington to know he has always been on the left. A week after Democrats swept the House and the Senate in the US midterms, the billionaire told Politico’s Playbook that he has “been a Democrat my whole life. ” He also said his company’s software, the same technology Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) relies on for Donald Trump’s deportation drive, is “essentially progressive.”“I grew up in a far left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir, all of our products are essentially progressive,” Karp said in the interview at Palantir’s Manhattan office. Politico counted him using the word “progressive” eight times. He said Democrats had “absolutely” corrected course in 2026, enough to win back his support for the 2028 presidential race.The timing has raised eyebrows. Karp put roughly $2 million into largely Republican causes during the first two years of Trump’s second term. That includes $1 million to the pro-Trump super PAC MAGA Inc. and another $1 million to Trump’s inauguration fund.Palantir is also among the donors paying for Trump’s new White House ballroom.Karp rejects the idea that he picked a side. “My giving is equal Democrat, Republican,” he told Politico. “I’m very balanced, and everyone in the political arena knows it.”There is a Democratic paper trail. Federal Election Commission records show Karp gave $360,000 to the joint fundraising committee for Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in 2023, and he endorsed Harris in 2024. In 2018, the Wall Street Journal referred to him as a “self-described socialist.”His recent record reads differently. Karp has called the Democratic Party “totally irresponsible,” described wokeness as a pagan religion and called Palantir the first company “to be completely anti-woke.” Meanwhile, Palantir became one of the Trump administration’s favourite contractors, with its tools helping ICE target people for removal. The company first started working with ICE under Barack Obama.Karp also welcomed Trump’s recent admission on 60 Minutes that the immigration crackdown may have gone too far. “I’m glad he’s saying in public now what I’ve been saying in private,” he said.He called the Republican losses a “referendum” on “economic justice.” He would back a Democrat in 2028, he said, as long as the candidate is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, the group that backed New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani.The new Congress is the real backdrop. Democrats take control of both chambers on January 3, which gives their committees the power to call hearings and subpoena executives. Senator Ed Markey has warned tech bosses they will need to “plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing.” Palantir, with deep ties to the Pentagon and ICE, is widely expected to draw scrutiny.Palantir has a lot riding on this. It reported $2.3 billion in revenue in its latest quarter, up 96% from a year ago, and government contracts make up a big part of the business.Karp insists his message is not about the company. “I’m really not pitching Palantir. I’m actually pitching, ‘What are you gonna do about economic justice in this country?’” he said.
Article Summary: Alex Karp calls Palantir’s products “essentially progressive” Karp says his political donations were always balanced between Democrats and Republicans. He would back a Democrat in 2028, he said, as long as the candidate is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America. Karp has called the Democratic Party “totally irresponsible’

Article Title: Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife MacKenzie Scott gave away $7 billion in 2025, accounting for more than one-third of America’s $19.2 billion in major charitable gifts
Article Text:
MacKenzie Scott's 2025 donation far outpaced other major philanthropists

American charitable giving reached $617.2 billion in 2025

Why Scott's name was missing from a major donor ranking

Earlier acts of kindness influenced her approach to giving

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Her Giving Pledge commitment has not stopped her wealth from growing

MacKenzie Scott’s approach to philanthropy has rarely followed the usual pattern of wealthy donors seeking public recognition for their contributions. Her donations often reach organisations without much advance publicity, and details of individual gifts can remain difficult to track. Yet the scale of her charitable giving became clear in figures covering America's largest donations in 2025. As reported by Fortune, Scott contributed around $7 billion during the year, representing roughly one- third of the $19.2 billion distributed through major charitable gifts. The amount also pushed her cumulative donations to $26.2 billion over five years, even as her personal fortune remained substantial.The figures, shared with Fortune by Giving USA and Indiana University's Lilly Family School of Philanthropy in June, placed Scott well ahead of other major donors in 2025. Her estimated $7 billion contribution accounted for the $19.2 billion classified as megagifts. Fortune reported other names among the year's biggest contributors included Michael Bloomberg, who gave $4.3 billion, and Bill Gates, whose donations reached $3.7 billion.Warren Buffett contributed approximately $1.34 billion, while Susan and Michael Dell together gave close to $1 billion.Scott's position was particularly striking because her giving was spread across thousands of organisations rather than concentrated in a handful of highly publicised projects.The largest gifts formed only part of a much wider increase in charitable contributions across the United States. Giving USA and the Lilly Family School of Philanthropy reported that total giving reached $617.2 billion in 2025, marking a 5.7% rise compared with the previous year.The estimate included contributions from individual donors, estates, charitable foundations and corporations to organisations working across the country. Religious institutions, human services, education and healthcare were among the major recipients, alongside international affairs groups and organisations supporting arts and culture.Gabe Cooper, vice chair of the Giving USA Foundation and founder and chief executive of Virtuous, said, “It was a positive year for charitable giving, with virtually all categories of recipient organizations achieving solid or better growth at the aggregate level.”Despite contributing billions of dollars, Scott did not appear on the Chronicle of Philanthropy's annual list of the 50 biggest donors. Her absence was not an indication that she had given less than other people featured in the ranking.The publication explained that Scott and her representatives had declined to provide information about her donations. It also pointed out that some contributions may have gone into donor-advised funds, making it difficult to establish whether they met the criteria used for its list.Scott has maintained a relatively private approach to her charitable activities. Unlike some wealthy philanthropists, she does not regularly publicise individual donations or provide detailed explanations of every organisation receiving money. Her donations are often announced by the organisations receiving them, rather than through a central public record released by Scott herself.Scott has previously described how experiences from her own life shaped her understanding of generosity. Some of the examples she has discussed involved relatively small amounts of money, but their effect on her circumstances was significant. During her college years, a roommate gave her $1,000 when she was facing the possibility of leaving her studies because of financial difficulties. She has also recalled a dentist who provided treatment without charging her after recognising that she could not afford the cost.These experiences became part of the thinking behind her philanthropic work. Rather than viewing generosity only through the amount of money transferred, Scott has written about how assistance can create consequences that extend far beyond the original act.In an essay published on 9 December, she reflected on how the effects of kindness can spread in ways that are difficult to measure. She questioned the assumption that contributions without an immediate financial return have limited value, suggesting that their wider benefits may not always be visible in conventional calculations. She has also written about the personal effects of giving. Referring to research into generosity and human behaviour, Scott noted that acts of kindness can activate pleasure-related areas of the brain and are associated with improved health and longer-term happiness.“It is these ripple effects that make imagining the power of any of our own acts of kindness impossible.”Scott's large-scale philanthropy accelerated following her 2019 divorce from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos. As part of the settlement, she received a substantial holding of Amazon shares, providing the financial resources behind much of her subsequent charitable activity.She later signed the Giving Pledge, a commitment made by some of the world's wealthiest individuals to give away most of their fortunes during their lifetimes or through their estates. Her donations have continued to reduce the amount of wealth she retains, although the value of her remaining assets has also been influenced by changes in Amazon's share price. By the time of the 2025 giving figures, her estimated net worth was still close to $37 billion.Her former husband Bezos has also made charitable contributions, although Scott's lifetime giving has been considerably larger relative to the amounts attributed to him.
Article Summary: American charitable giving reached $617.2 billion in 2025. MacKenzie Scott's 2025 donation far outpaced other major philanthropists. Scott did not appear on the Chronicle of Philanthropy's annual list of the 50 biggest donors. Her absence was not an indication that she had given less than other people.

Article Title: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry says: There was always a 'big worry 'at Nvidia, as CEO Jensen Huang never ...

Michael Burry believes Nvidia's dependence on Huang was always a concern

Gene Munster remains bullish on Nvidia

Demand for AI chips seen outweighing leadership concerns

America’s biggest investor Michael Burry, who is famous for predicting the 2008 housing market crash has once again raised concerns about Nvidia’s dependence on CEO Jensen Huang, arguing that the AI chip giant has long faced a significant ‘key-man-risk’ because of Huang’s rile in the company. Burry made the fresh comments amid the ongoing scrutiny of Huang. The Nvidia CEO is reportedly facing a broad investigation over the allegations of extra-marital affairs, starting a fresh debate on succession planning at Nvidia and also the company’s ability to seamlessly navigate a leadership transition.In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Burry declared that "The Don has fallen," describing Huang as an "Enforcer" while referencing reports surrounding a Department of Justice probe. He pointed to reports that the Nvidia chief executive oversaw roughly 60 direct reports and delegated little responsibility, arguing that the company's heavy reliance on one executive had been a long-standing concern. "The key-man risk at NVIDIA always was a worry," Burry wrote, while expressing scepticism that chief financial officer Colette Kress could seamlessly assume leadership of the company if required.Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, believes that despite the leadership uncertainty, Nvidia’s competitive position remains intact due to the overwhelming demand for AI chips. Speaking in an interview with CNBC, Muster emphasised that he initially expected the Nvidia shared to suffer a massive decline amid the on going controversy, but he feels that the investors will ultimately refocus on the business fundamentals of the company."I would expect that the stock probably gaps down and then starts to slowly work higher," he said.Muster further rejected the idea that rival companies like AMD stand a chance to gain materially from the issues at Nvidia, as Nvidia’s products still remain the preferred choice for major cloud and AI companies. Article Summary: Michael Burry believes Nvidia's dependence on CEO Jensen Huang was always a concern. Gene Munster remains bullish on Nvidia despite leadership uncertainty. Customers will still prioritise Nvidia’s advanced AI hardware regardless of the fact that who is heading the company.

Article Title: United Airlines bans AI Agents from booking tickets; tell customers: We have a problem with …
Article Text:
United Airlines bans AI Agents from booking tickets; tell customers: We have a problem with …

Why does United Airlines have a problem with AI agents

United Airlines wants to keep control of flight bookings

United Airlines has banned AI agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers. The US airline said on November 11 that it is restricting artificial intelligence agents from booking tickets, citing security risks and concerns that some actions taken by these tools could violate federal rules. The move comes as more people turn to AI agents to handle everyday tasks, including researching products, finding deals and making purchases. Tools such as Meta’s Muse and OpenAI ’s dots are designed to complete tasks on behalf of users, rather than simply answer questions.However, United Airlines has raised concerns about allowing these agents to access its booking systems and customers’ personal information. The airline said sharing account credentials with third-party AI assistants could expose sensitive information and lead to unintended purchases, changes to accounts or the use of MileagePlus miles.Booking a flight through an AI agent may require access to a traveler’s personal details, account login information and payment credentials. United Airlines said this could create security risks if an AI assistant makes a booking or changes an account without the user’s intended action.The airline also warned that certain activities carried out by AI agents, such as checking in passengers, could violate federal regulations.For example, some rules require travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain prohibited substances.“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said.United is also updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new restrictions. The airline’s decision could also be linked to its efforts to retain control over how customers search for and book flights.Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group, told CBS News that United does not want to add another powerful intermediary to the booking process."United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. Article Title: Amazon to refund $3 million to Prime customers over six-step cancellation process; also to donate $1 million to charities and $1.5 million to consumer education and fraud investigation fund for AG's o
Article Text:
Amazon denies violating laws

Allegations centred on ' dark patterns '

Terms of the settlement

The six-step process

Link to the FTC deal

Another lawsuit pending

Amazon has agreed to refund $3 million to eligible Arizona consumers and make additional payments totalling $4 million as part of a settlement with the Arizona Attorney General's Office over allegations that the company made it unnecessarily difficult for customers to cancel their Prime memberships, according to a report by Moneywise. Amazon denied any wrongdoing as part of the agreement. The settlement stems from a lawsuit filed by Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes in 2024, which accused the e-commerce giant of using "unfair and deceptive business practices" in its Prime cancellation process. According to the complaint, customers were required to navigate through at least six steps to cancel their subscriptions before changes were made in 2023.While agreeing to the settlement, Amazon maintained that it had not violated Arizona law. The company "denies that it ever engaged in activity that violates any Arizona law," according to the settlement cited in reports. The Arizona case follows broader regulatory scrutiny of Amazon's Prime subscription practices. In 2025, the company settled a separate lawsuit brought by the US Federal Trade Commission over allegations that consumers were enrolled in Prime without consent and faced obstacles when attempting to cancel.That settlement included a $2.5 billion payment and commitments to simplify subscription sign-up and cancellation processes. The latest agreement adds to growing pressure on subscription-based businesses to make cancellations as straightforward as enrolment, amid ongoing debates in the US over consumer protection and so-called "click-to-cancel" rules.Arizona officials alleged that Amazon employed what are known as "dark patterns" - design tactics that can influence consumer behaviour through confusing interfaces, repeated prompts and misleading wording. The lawsuit claimed that the company's cancellation process, internally referred to as "Project Iliad," was intentionally designed to discourage users from ending their memberships. The state said consumers had to work through a complicated series of screens and prompts before being allowed to cancel Prime, making the process more difficult than necessaryUnder the consent judgment, the $3 million goes to the Attorney General’s Office to be distributed to “eligible consumers.” According to spokesman Richie Taylor, these are people who tried to end their $139-a-year Prime membership but ran into hurdles that Mayes says were purposely designed to make cancellation difficult.Amazon will also:•pay $1.5 million into a separate fund the attorney general’s office uses to investigate consumer fraud and teach Arizonans how to protect themselves•pay another $1.5 million to cover the state’s legal fees•donate $1 million to organisations selected by Mayes, all of which provide food to people in needAmazon denies that it engaged in any activity that violates Arizona law. The state’s attorneys agreed they cannot claim that any of Amazon’s past, present or future business practices are illegal.Mayes sued in 2024. Her complaint said that until 2023, Amazon used a system that required at least six separate actions to cancel Prime online, despite advertising that customers could “cancel anytime.” The steps were to log in to Prime Central, click “manage membership,” go to “end membership,” click “continue to cancel” twice, and then click “end now.” Mayes said the system was a success for Amazon. At one point it reduced cancellations by 14% as fewer members reached the final cancellation page, she said in legal filings. The process was never disclosed to people signing up, she said. Prime members spend an average of $1,400 a year on purchases, more than double the spending of non-Prime customers, and Amazon collects $25 billion a year in Prime fees, about three-quarters of it from the US, according to her filings.Amazon agreed to change its cancellation practices last year in a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission that included a $1 billion civil penalty and $1.5 billion in refunds. Mayes pressed on with her own suit under Arizona’s consumer fraud law. Taylor said it is unclear whether the FTC settlement covers everyone who faced the cancellation hassles and all their costs. “Our goal is to get as much back to consumers as possible,” he said.“Arizonans should be able to cancel a subscription as easily as they signed up for it, without jumping through endless hoops,” Mayes said in a statement. She said the settlement provides restitution to eligible Arizonans and that her office will keep standing up for consumers stuck with subscriptions they never intended to keep.A second 2024 suit by Mayes against Amazon, over how it lists products on its website, is still being fought in Maricopa County Superior Court. She alleges that the “Buy Box” algorithm favours offers that earn Amazon the highest fees, so shoppers often overpay. Amazon has denied violating any laws and said the suit mischaracterises how its businesses work. No hearing date has been set.
Article Summary: Settlement stems from a lawsuit filed by Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes in 2024. She accused the e-commerce giant of using "unfair and deceptive business practices" in its Prime cancellation process. According to the complaint, customers were required to navigate through at least six steps to cancel their subscriptions before changes were made in 2023.

Article Title: Jamie Dimon warns, as AI companies ‘boast’ their Agents can do a lot including making payments for customers; says: Don’t allow that as they will …

AI is moving ‘more like a Tsunami’

As artificial intelligence (AI) developers boast that autonomous agents can manage personal errands, book travel, and even execute purchases, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon is urging consumers and financial institutions not to allow AI agents to handle direct banking payments. Speaking at The Economic Club of Chicago this week, Dimon cautioned that authorising a software agent to execute payments requires handing over sensitive banking codes and if done, it is effectively inviting unvetted algorithms deep inside personal accounts with no promise that it will protect your best interests.“That means they are in your bank and you’re assuming they’re going to act properly on your behalf and they may not,” Dimon said, warning that autonomous agents could carry out actions that prove “treacherous” for financial institutions.Dimon’s comments arrive amid rapid commercial adoption of consumer-facing AI agents that are capable of managing personal calendars, drafting emails and coordinating travel bookings. The JPMorgan chief previously sounded alarms during the bank’s third-quarter earnings call, warning that the financial system could soon contend with thousands of rogue agents. Dimon noted that autonomous tools may execute round-the-clock cyber intrusions or trigger vulnerabilities if granted access to consumer accounts.Despite the warnings, JPMorgan is advancing its own controlled implementations. Company CFO Jeremy Barnum confirmed that the lender’s proprietary Smart Cash tool, which has been built to help clients oversee and balance liquidity across multiple accounts, is currently undergoing an early-stage pilot. JPMorgan has used AI internally since 2012 across functions including risk assessment, fraud prevention, marketing, credit underwriting, and customer support.Drawing historical parallels, Dimon compared the rapid rise of AI to the Industrial Revolution, but noted that modern computing shifts are occurring at high speeds. Calling the rapid spread of the technology “more like a tsunami” that cannot be stopped, Dimon argued that public institutions and corporate leaders must move quickly to contain digital fallout: “You can’t stop it. You just have to, like, manage the hell out of it.With open-source releases and systems originating worldwide, Dimon emphasised that global governments cannot simply halt model proliferation. The technology’s acceleration is backed by massive capital flows, with tech giants Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta planning more than $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, primarily dedicated to AI infrastructure.Recently, JP Morgan Chase, Citi Bank and Bank of America ‘banned’ AI agents from logging into customer accounts and moving money. They fear that the software could initiate uncontrolled cash movements and erode vital deposit bases.

Authorising a software agent to execute payments requires handing over sensitive banking codes.
